home-energy-audit.title: Home energy audits in Hamilton: EnerGuide evaluations, costs and rebates
home-energy-audit.description: Book an EnerGuide home energy audit in Hamilton: 26 licensed organizations, local prices, Ontario rebates and what 69% pre-1991 housing means for your upgrade list.
home-energy-audit.lede: 26 NRCan-licensed service organizations deliver EnerGuide home evaluations in Hamilton. Here's what one costs, what it tends to find in Hamilton houses, and which Ontario rebates it unlocks.

sections.h2: What an evaluation finds in Hamilton homes
sections.html:
Of Hamilton's 167,240 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 34% were built before 1961 and 69% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. The typical Hamilton house dates from 1971–1980, and an evaluation is how you find out what that means for yours: the blower door measures air leakage, the advisor inspects the attic, walls, basement, windows and heating system, and the report ranks upgrades by what they'd save.

Hamilton gets about 3,449 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −15.6°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Burlington Piers. That's about 12% less heating demand than the middle of the 70 cities we cover. The more heating a climate needs, the more each fix is worth, which is why the evaluation's ranked list matters more in some cities than others.

In the Hamilton area, 75% of households heat mainly with a forced-air furnace; natural gas is the main heating energy for 65% of households and electricity for 20% (Statistics Canada, 2023). The heating system on the report shapes the recommendations: a forced-air furnace invites a ducted heat pump, electric baseboards a ductless one.

Windfall Ecology Centre, one of the few Ontario providers that publishes prices, charges $500 + HST for the initial evaluation and $250 + HST for the follow-up; Reep Green Solutions lists $540. City-backed programs in Ottawa and London quote $500–$700 as typical.

Most providers quote the initial (pre-upgrade) and follow-up (post-upgrade) visits separately. Rebate programs that pay on measured improvement need both, so ask for the combined price.

• Initial evaluation, about 2–3 hours. The advisor measures and inspects the house and runs the blower door test.
  • Report and EnerGuide rating. You get the home's energy rating in gigajoules per year and a list of recommended upgrades with estimated savings.
  • Do the work. Most rebate programs only count upgrades done after the initial evaluation.
  • Follow-up evaluation. A second visit measures the improvement, which is what most rebates pay on.

heat-loss-calculation.title: Heat loss calculation in Hamilton: sizing a heat pump for −15.6°C
heat-loss-calculation.description: A CSA F280 room-by-room heat loss calculation for Hamilton homes, sized to the local −15.6°C design temperature: why it matters for heat pumps, what it costs and who does it.
heat-loss-calculation.lede: The heat loss calculation is how a heat pump or furnace gets sized for your house, and the key input is the design temperature: −15.6°C for Hamilton, from NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Burlington Piers.

sections.h2: Why the design temperature matters in Hamilton
sections.html:
−15.6°C is the 18th-mildest design temperature of the 70 cities we cover. The F280 calculation works out how much heat each room loses on that design day, from the house's actual walls, windows, air leakage and ceiling insulation.

At −15.6°C, a cold-climate heat pump sized to the calculation can carry most of the season, and the number shows how much backup heat the coldest days need.

In the Hamilton area, 75% of households heat mainly with a forced-air furnace; natural gas is the main heating energy for 65% of households and electricity for 20% (Statistics Canada, 2023).

Contractors who size by square footage routinely oversize. An oversized heat pump costs more to buy, cycles on and off, dehumidifies poorly in summer and wears faster. An undersized one leans on backup heat. The F280 report is the evidence either way, and it's worth having before you compare quotes.

About $150–$400 as a standalone calculation (a September 2026 planning range; quotes vary). Many energy advisors bundle it with an EnerGuide evaluation, which also gives the calculation measured air-leakage data instead of an assumption.

providers.heading: NRCan-licensed service organizations serving Hamilton
providers.note: Many energy advisors also do room-by-room CSA F280 calculations for an extra fee; HVAC designers do them too. Ask for the F280 report itself, not just an equipment recommendation.

ventilation-assessment.lede: Condensation on windows, musty basements and stuffy bedrooms are ventilation and humidity problems, and they're easy to confuse with insulation problems. A ventilation assessment measures which one you have.

sections.h2: Why Hamilton homes get humidity problems
sections.html:
Hamilton gets about 3,449 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −15.6°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Burlington Piers. On Hamilton's coldest days, window glass and poorly insulated corners get cold enough for condensation at humidity levels that feel normal indoors, so winter humidity needs to stay at the lower end of the comfortable range.

Of Hamilton's 167,240 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 34% were built before 1961 and 69% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Newer houses (21% of Hamilton's were built since 2001) are tight and usually have an HRV or ERV that needs balancing and cleaning. Older houses that get air-sealed can lose the accidental ventilation they used to rely on.

• Relative humidity in living areas and the basement.
  • Actual airflow from bath and kitchen fans, and whether they vent outside rather than into the attic.
  • How much fresh air the house gets, and whether an HRV or ERV is balanced.

energy-bill-analysis.title: Energy bill analysis in Hamilton: getting 12 months of usage from Alectra Utilities
energy-bill-analysis.description: How to pull 12 months of usage from Alectra Utilities / Hydro One and Enbridge Gas and turn it into a weather-normalized baseline for Hamilton's 3,449 heating degree-days.
energy-bill-analysis.lede: Your own bills are the most accurate starting point for any energy plan. In Hamilton, that means electricity from Alectra Utilities / Hydro One and natural gas from Enbridge Gas.

sections.h2: Getting your usage history in Hamilton
sections.html:
Most of Hamilton is served by Alectra Utilities / Hydro One for electricity and Enbridge Gas for natural gas.

  • Alectra Utilities: My Alectra account, then Green Button: download or connect electricity usage, billing and account data (XML). Interval-metered businesses also get a CSV energy-usage portal with 24 months of data. Link
  • Hydro One: myAccount, then Green Button Download My Data: up to 24 months of billing, consumption and transaction data (XML). Link
  • Enbridge Gas: Gas utility (most of Ontario): My Account, then Share My Data, then Download your Data: up to 24 months of billing and usage data as Green Button XML. Link

Hamilton gets about 3,449 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −15.6°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Burlington Piers. Weather-normalizing your bills against those degree-days separates heating from baseload (lights, appliances, hot water), so you can see how much of the bill a heating upgrade can actually touch, and compare a mild year with a harsh one fairly.

radon-testing.title: Radon testing in Hamilton: local levels, test kits and certified professionals
radon-testing.description: Radon in Hamilton: Health Canada survey results for the City of Hamilton Health Unit region (5% above the guideline), how to test for 3+ months, where to get kits and C-NRPP professionals locally.
radon-testing.lede: Radon is invisible, has no smell, and is the second-leading cause of lung cancer in Canada. In Health Canada's national survey, 5% of homes tested in the City of Hamilton Health Unit health region were above the guideline, and the only way to know about your house is to test it.

glance.sub: the Hamilton, ON (Hamilton CMA) metro area

sections.html:
Health Canada's 2012 survey found 5% of 100 homes tested in the City of Hamilton Health Unit health region above the guideline. The larger 2024 Cross-Canada survey reports 12.0% (1 in 8) of houses at or above the guideline for the Hamilton, ON (Hamilton CMA) metro area.

The two surveys aren't directly comparable: the 2024 study pooled about 69,000 volunteer tests and more of them were taken in basements, which partly explains its higher numbers. Neither can tell you about a single house, because neighbouring homes can differ widely.

• Use a long-term test of at least three months, with most of it in the heating season, which gives the most conservative result.
  • Place the detector in the lowest level you spend four or more hours a day in, away from drafts, and follow the kit's instructions.
  • If the result is above 200 Bq/m³, Health Canada recommends fixing it within a year, sooner if it's much higher.

Our full radon testing guide.

• There's no provincial free-kit program, but many Ontario public libraries lend digital radon monitors free with a library card, among them Hamilton, Vaughan, Guelph, Kingston Frontenac, Greater Sudbury, Thunder Bay, Brantford and Waterloo.
  • For a professional measurement or mitigation, search the C-NRPP directory by your Hamilton postal code; it lists certified measurement and mitigation professionals.

• Since January 1, 2025, the Ontario Building Code requires new houses to include a soil-gas barrier and a radon rough-in.
  • Tarion's new-home warranty covers radon remediation for seven years from possession, and the Canadian Lung Association's Lungs Matter program offers up to $1,500 toward mitigation for households with low to moderate incomes or a lung cancer diagnosis.
  • If your level is high, mitigation (usually a sub-slab depressurization fan system installed by a C-NRPP-certified professional) typically costs $2,000–$4,000.

faq.q: Is radon a problem in Hamilton?
faq.a: Health Canada's 2012 survey found 5% of 100 homes tested in the City of Hamilton Health Unit health region above the guideline. The larger 2024 Cross-Canada survey reports 12.0% (1 in 8) of houses at or above the guideline for the Hamilton, ON (Hamilton CMA) metro area. Any home can have high radon, so Health Canada recommends testing every home.

faq.q: How long should a radon test take?
faq.a: At least three months, with most of it during the heating season. Short tests can't tell you your long-term average.

faq.q: Where can I get a radon test kit in Hamilton?
faq.a: There's no provincial free-kit program, but many Ontario public libraries lend digital radon monitors free with a library card, among them Hamilton, Vaughan, Guelph, Kingston Frontenac, Greater Sudbury, Thunder Bay, Brantford and Waterloo. Hardware stores and lung associations also sell long-term kits for about $30–$60.

faq.q: What does radon mitigation cost?
faq.a: Typically $2,000–$4,000 for a sub-slab depressurization system installed by a C-NRPP-certified professional.

carbon-monoxide-testing.title: Carbon monoxide testing in Hamilton: the Ontario alarm rules and appliance checks
carbon-monoxide-testing.description: CO safety for Hamilton homes: what Ontario law requires, why it matters with 65% of households heating with natural gas, where alarms go and how appliances get checked.
carbon-monoxide-testing.lede: Carbon monoxide is odourless and can kill. Ontario's Fire Code requires CO alarms in existing homes that have a fuel-burning appliance, a fireplace or an attached garage: next to every sleeping area and, since January 1, 2026, on every storey as well.

sections.html: Ontario's Fire Code requires CO alarms in existing homes that have a fuel-burning appliance, a fireplace or an attached garage: next to every sleeping area and, since January 1, 2026, on every storey as well.

In the Hamilton area, the main heating energy is natural gas for 65% of households (Statistics Canada, 2023). Any fuel-burning appliance, fireplace or attached garage is a potential CO source.

Single-detached houses make up 56% of Hamilton's households; many have an attached garage, another reason to put an alarm near the door into the house.

• Alarms next to sleeping areas and on every storey, tested monthly and replaced by their end-of-life date (usually 7 to 10 years).
  • Annual service of fuel-burning appliances by a licensed technician.
  • A combustion spillage test during an energy evaluation, which catches a venting problem before it produces CO.

Our carbon monoxide guide · Combustion safety testing in Hamilton

faq.q: Are carbon monoxide alarms mandatory in Hamilton?
faq.a: Ontario's Fire Code requires CO alarms in existing homes that have a fuel-burning appliance, a fireplace or an attached garage: next to every sleeping area and, since January 1, 2026, on every storey as well.

faq.q: Where should CO alarms go?
faq.a: Outside every sleeping area and on every storey, following the manufacturer's instructions. Some rules also call for one near a fuel-burning appliance or the door from an attached garage.

faq.q: How long do CO alarms last?
faq.a: Most have an end-of-life date of 7 to 10 years printed on the unit; replace them by then even if they still beep when tested.

mold-testing.h1: Mold and air quality testing in Hamilton
mold-testing.title: Mold testing in Hamilton: air quality sampling and finding the moisture source
mold-testing.description: Mold and indoor air quality testing in Hamilton: when sampling is worth $300–$600, why cold winters cause condensation, and how to find an accredited lab.
mold-testing.lede: Mold sampling tells you whether there's a hidden mold problem and roughly where. It doesn't tell you why, and fixing the moisture source is the actual cure.

sections.h2: Why mold shows up in Hamilton homes
sections.html:
Hamilton gets about 3,449 heating degree-days a year and has a winter design temperature of −15.6°C, according to NRCan's HOT2000 climate data for Burlington Piers. On cold days, exterior corners, closets on outside walls and window frames get cold enough for condensation, which is where mold usually starts in Hamilton houses.

Of Hamilton's 167,240 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 34% were built before 1961 and 69% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census. Older basements without a moisture barrier and houses that were air-sealed without adding ventilation are common trouble spots.

• You smell mustiness but can't find the source.
  • After a leak or flood, to check that cleanup worked.
  • Before buying an older house with signs of past water damage.

If you can see mould, you usually don't need a test to know it's there; you need to fix the moisture and clean it up properly.

No Canadian province has a mandatory mould standard for homes. Health Canada's guideline sets no numerical limit: it says to fix moisture problems and clean up visible mould.

Ask any Hamilton tester which lab analyzes their samples, and look for one accredited under AIHA's EMLAP program for environmental microbiology. Pair sampling with a ventilation and humidity assessment, which finds the cause.

Ventilation and humidity assessments in Hamilton · Our mold and indoor air quality guide

faq.q: How much does mold testing cost in Hamilton?
faq.a: Plan on about $300–$600 for a typical sampling visit (a September 2026 planning range); lab fees for extra samples add to that.

faq.q: Do I need a test if I can see mould?
faq.a: Usually not. Visible mould needs cleanup and a fix for the moisture source. Testing helps most when you suspect mould you can't see.

faq.q: Is there a legal mould limit for homes in Canada?
faq.a: No. Health Canada sets no numerical limit; its guidance is to control moisture and clean up mould. Quebec has a voluntary handling standard.

asbestos-testing.h1: Asbestos and vermiculite testing in Hamilton
asbestos-testing.title: Asbestos testing in Hamilton: vermiculite, labs and the Ontario rules
asbestos-testing.description: Asbestos and vermiculite testing in Hamilton, where 69% of houses were built before 1991: what to sample, lab costs and the Ontario rules for renovation.
asbestos-testing.lede: About 114,900 Hamilton houses (69%) were built before 1991, when asbestos still turned up in insulation, flooring, plaster and duct wrap. A lab test before renovation is the only way to know.

sections.h2: Where asbestos shows up in Hamilton houses
sections.html:
Of Hamilton's 167,240 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 34% were built before 1961 and 69% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census.

  • Vermiculite attic insulation: loose, pebbly, grey-brown or silver-gold granules.
  • Vinyl floor tiles and their adhesive, textured ceilings and some plaster.
  • Duct wrap and pipe insulation on older heating systems.

In Ontario, O. Reg. 278/05 sets the rules for contractors working with asbestos. Owners must have materials checked before arranging renovation or demolition work, but that duty doesn't apply to an owner-occupied house or a building of four units or fewer, so testing your own home is your decision.

Whatever the rules, don't sand, cut or remove suspect material yourself before it's tested.

A trained assessor takes small samples, and an accredited lab analyzes them; plan on about $50–$150 per sample. Asbestos labs in Canada are typically accredited under NIST's NVLAP program.

Our asbestos and vermiculite guide · Attic inspections in Hamilton

faq.q: Do I need an asbestos test before renovating in Hamilton?
faq.a: If the house was built before 1991 and the work will disturb insulation, flooring, plaster or duct wrap, test first. In Ontario, O. Reg. 278/05 sets the rules for contractors working with asbestos. Owners must have materials checked before arranging renovation or demolition work, but that duty doesn't apply to an owner-occupied house or a building of four units or fewer, so testing your own home is your decision.

faq.q: How much does asbestos testing cost?
faq.a: About $50–$150 per lab sample, plus the assessor's visit. Abatement, if needed, is quoted separately.

faq.q: What should I do if I have vermiculite in the attic?
faq.a: Leave it alone, keep the attic closed, and have it sampled before any attic work. Health Canada advises against disturbing it or removing it yourself.

lead-paint-testing.title: Lead paint testing in Hamilton: which homes are at risk and how to test
lead-paint-testing.description: 34% of Hamilton's houses were built before 1961, when lead paint was common. How to test with $15–$40 swabs or a lab, and how to renovate safely.
lead-paint-testing.lede: Health Canada says a home built before 1960 probably has lead paint somewhere. That's 34% of Hamilton's houses (built before 1961, per the 2021 Census), plus exterior paint on many of the 35% built from 1961 to 1990.

sections.h2: Which Hamilton homes are at risk
sections.html:
Of Hamilton's 167,240 houses (single-detached, semi-detached, row houses and duplexes), 34% were built before 1961 and 69% before 1991, according to the 2021 Census.

  • Built before 1960: probably has lead-based paint (Health Canada).
  • Built 1960–1990: exterior paint may contain lead, and interior paint may contain smaller amounts.
  • Built after 1990: consumer paints were virtually lead-free by then.

• Swab kits ($15–$40) give a quick screen of the surfaces you plan to disturb.
  • For certainty, send paint chips to a lab accredited under AIHA's ELLAP program, or hire a firm with an X-ray fluorescence (XRF) analyzer.
  • Test before sanding, stripping or replacing old windows and trim.

Our lead paint guide.

Don't dry-sand, use a heat gun or power-wash it. Contain the work area, mist surfaces, clean with a HEPA vacuum, and keep children and pregnant people away until cleanup is done. No province has a lead-paint rule aimed at homeowners, but contractors in B.C. and Yukon must include lead in pre-renovation or demolition hazard inspections.

faq.q: Does my Hamilton house have lead paint?
faq.a: If it was built before 1960, probably; 1960–1990, possibly on the exterior. Test the surfaces you plan to disturb.

faq.q: Are lead test swabs reliable?
faq.a: They are a useful screen. For renovation decisions, confirm with a lab analysis of paint chips or an XRF reading.

faq.q: What does lead paint testing cost?
faq.a: Swab kits run about $15–$40; lab analysis and XRF testing cost more and are quoted by the firm.

well-water-testing.title: Well water testing in Hamilton: how to test and what it costs in Ontario
well-water-testing.description: Private well water testing in Hamilton: many homes outside the piped areas use private wells. How Ontario's testing program works, what it costs and how often to test.
well-water-testing.lede: The City of Hamilton estimates about 10,000 private wells and cisterns are in use, mainly by rural residents. If yours is, here's how testing works in Ontario.

sections.html:
The City of Hamilton estimates about 10,000 private wells and cisterns are in use, mainly by rural residents.

Local program: City of Hamilton Residential Well Decommissioning Grant: 100% of the cost up to $1,000 per well (max. 2 wells per property) to plug unused wells. Hamilton Public Health Services recommends bacteria testing at least three times a year. Details

Free bacteria testing through Public Health Ontario labs: pick up a kit at a PHO lab or your public health unit and drop it back off. Chemistry (nitrate, sodium, metals) goes to a licensed private lab for a fee. Local health units recommend testing at least three times a year: spring, summer and fall.

• Bacteria (total coliforms and E. coli): at least once a year, and after flooding, heavy rain or work on the well.
  • Nitrate, especially near farmland or septic systems.
  • Metals and naturally occurring contaminants such as arsenic, uranium or manganese when a well is new and every few years after, depending on local geology.

Our well water guide.

faq.q: Is well water testing free in Ontario?
faq.a: Free bacteria testing through Public Health Ontario labs: pick up a kit at a PHO lab or your public health unit and drop it back off. Chemistry (nitrate, sodium, metals) goes to a licensed private lab for a fee. Local health units recommend testing at least three times a year: spring, summer and fall.

faq.q: How often should I test my well?
faq.a: For bacteria, at least once a year and after flooding, heavy rain or well work; many health units recommend more often. Test chemistry when the well is new and every few years after.

faq.q: Are private wells common in Hamilton?
faq.a: The City of Hamilton estimates about 10,000 private wells and cisterns are in use, mainly by rural residents.

commercial-energy-audit.title: Commercial energy audits in Hamilton: reporting rules and incentives
commercial-energy-audit.description: Commercial and multi-unit building energy audits in Hamilton: ASHRAE levels, 2 reporting rules that apply, and 5 utility or government incentives for audits and studies.
commercial-energy-audit.lede: Offices, apartment buildings, retail and industrial sites get engineering energy audits rather than EnerGuide evaluations. Here's what applies in Hamilton: 2 mandatory reporting rules and 5 incentive programs we found for audits and studies.

sections.h2: Reporting rules that apply in Hamilton
sections.html:
• No city-specific rule found (none found): No municipal energy/water benchmarking, reporting or building-performance by-law found; provincial rules apply (see rules.provinces.ON).
  • Energy and Water Reporting and Benchmarking (EWRB) - O. Reg. 506/18 (in force): Buildings 50,000 sq ft (4,645 m2) and larger. Buildings 100,000 sq ft and larger need a certified professional to verify data in the first reporting year and every five years after. Source
  • Broader Public Sector energy reporting - O. Reg. 25/23 (in force): Applies by organization type (public agencies), not floor area. Source

• Commercial Custom Audits & Studies - Energy Assessments and Meters (Enbridge Gas (Ontario)): Pays up to 50% of eligible costs for energy audits, engineering feasibility studies, steam trap surveys/audits, air and water balancing and metering. The cap depends on the address's previous-year gas use: up to $6,000 (100,000 to under 3,000,000 m3), up to $10,000 (3,000,000 to under 10,000,000 m3), up to $20,000 (10,000,000 m3+, institutions only). Institutions max $20,000 per project; other commercial sectors max $10,000 per project. Details
  • Affordable Housing Multi-Residential Program - energy assessment (Enbridge Gas (Ontario)): Up to $8,000 for an energy assessment (up to $40,000 per housing provider) to find natural gas savings in affordable housing buildings. Details
  • Save on Energy Small Business Program (Save on Energy (IESO)): Free on-site assessment by qualified Save on Energy representatives, then free installed upgrades: up to $3,000 for lighting and up to $2,500 for refrigeration and smart thermostats (up to $5,500 total). Details
  • Existing Building Commissioning (EBCx) Program (Save on Energy (IESO)): Funds retro-commissioning. Investigation phase: up to $0.06 per sq ft, max $50,000 per application or 75% of the participant's cost for the commissioning provider. Implementation and persistence phases: $0.03 per kWh of confirmed/persisting savings (each capped at 30% of annual consumption or $50,000, whichever is lower). Details
  • XLerate Program - Project Feasibility Study funding (Save on Energy (IESO)): Project feasibility study (PFS) funding at a 50% cost share; project incentives of $300/MWh up to 75% of eligible costs (max $15 million per project). Details

• Level 1, walk-through: a site visit and bill review that benchmarks the building and lists low-cost measures.
  • Level 2, energy survey and analysis: where the energy goes, with savings and cost estimates per measure. Most incentive applications use this level.
  • Level 3, detailed analysis: monitoring and modelling for capital-intensive projects.

Ask which level a quote covers. Audits are done by engineering firms and energy consultants; look for a P.Eng. and credentials such as the Certified Energy Manager (CEM). How commercial energy audits work.

faq.q: Do Hamilton buildings have to report energy use?
faq.a: Yes, above certain sizes: Energy and Water Reporting and Benchmarking (EWRB) - O. Reg. 506/18; Broader Public Sector energy reporting - O. Reg. 25/23.

faq.q: Are there incentives for commercial energy audits in Hamilton?
faq.a: Yes: Commercial Custom Audits & Studies - Energy Assessments and Meters; Affordable Housing Multi-Residential Program - energy assessment; Save on Energy Small Business Program; Existing Building Commissioning (EBCx) Program. Check eligibility and pre-approval rules before you commission the audit.

faq.q: What does a commercial energy audit cost?
faq.a: It depends on the building's size and the ASHRAE level. Get quotes that state the level and the deliverables.
